addmaths-0606-count-factorial-notation.description: Simplify factorial ratios and justify the product rule.

sections.title: What changes when a place is filled?
sections.label: Successive places

blocks.html: Multiply the number of options at each stage. Filling a position removes one option from the remaining supply.

figure.alt: Slot 1 has six choices, slot 2 has five choices, and slot 3 has four choices.
figure.caption: Six distinct objects fill three labelled slots. Each choice removes one object from the supply.

blocks.title: Practise the method
blocks.html: Write the choices for each position over a row of empty boxes. If all n positions are filled with distinct objects, the product is \(n!\).

blocks.title: Use the product rule to arrange distinct objects
blocks.prompt: Distinct books are placed on a shelf from left to right. There are 10 objects. How many orders are possible with no restriction?
blocks.hint: After each position is filled there is one fewer choice.
blocks.solution:
There are 10 choices for the first place, 9 for the next, and so on down to one.

Multiply these choices to obtain \(10!\).

Answer: \(3628800\).

retry.feedback: There are different numbers of choices at each stage. The supply shrinks after each choice.

blocks.html: Adding the numbers of options misses the combinations of consecutive choices.

blocks.title: Count ordered selections
blocks.prompt: A workshop has 12 distinct speaker applications. In how many ways can the organiser assign the 4 numbered speaking slots? A candidate or item may be used only once.
blocks.hint: Swapping two occupied places produces a different result.
blocks.solution:
The slots are different, so use \({}^{12}P_{4}\).

Compute \(\frac{12!}{8!}\).

Answer: \(11880\).

retry.feedback: That counts sets of choices. Changing the order here changes the result.

blocks.html: Name what is being counted in each factor. Multiply successive choices and add only disjoint alternatives.

sections.title: How much of a factorial do I expand?
sections.label: Cancel factors

blocks.html: Expand only to the largest common factorial, then cancel it.

blocks.title: Practise the method
blocks.html: Treat \(0!\) as one empty arrangement. For a longer numerator, step down one factor at a time.

blocks.title: Cancel a factorial quotient
blocks.prompt: Evaluate \(\frac{6!}{2!}\).
blocks.hint: Expand the numerator only as far as the factorial in the denominator.
blocks.solution:
The common factor is \(2!\). Cancel it.

Multiply the remaining factors: \(6\times5\times4\times3\).

Answer: \(360\).

retry.feedback: The factor immediately below the last required factor belongs to the cancelled denominator.

blocks.html: Cancel factors of the whole product. A factorial does not distribute over addition.

blocks.title: Simplify a factorial expression
blocks.hint: Expand only the longer factorial. Remember the empty arrangement.
blocks.solution:
Write \((10+1)!=(10+1)10!\). Cancel the common factorial.

The remaining terms are \(11+1\), since \(0!=1\).

Answer: \(12\).

retry.feedback: The factorial ratio is correct. The additional term is one.

blocks.html: Name what is being counted in each factor. Multiply successive choices and add only disjoint alternatives.

sections.title: How can I solve a factorial equation?
sections.label: Work back

blocks.html: Cancel first, then solve the smaller polynomial equation.

blocks.title: Practise the method
blocks.html: Check that each resulting factorial argument is a non-negative integer. Use the context to choose a valid root.

blocks.title: Find the integer in a factorial equation
blocks.prompt: Find the non-negative integer \(r\) for which \(\frac{(r+2)!}{r!}=156\).
blocks.hint: The factorial ratio leaves two consecutive factors.
blocks.solution:
Expand and cancel to obtain \((r+2)(r+1)=156\).

The two consecutive factors are \(12\) and \(13\). The other algebraic root is negative.

Answer: \(11\).

retry.feedback: The smaller factor is one more than the requested value.

blocks.html: An algebraic root may lie outside the factorial domain.

blocks.title: Recover the group size from ordered pairs
blocks.prompt: There are 56 ways to name a first and second person from a group of \(n\) distinct people. Determine \(n\).
blocks.hint: There are n choices first and one fewer second.
blocks.solution:
Use \(n(n-1)=56\).

The roots are \(8\) and \(-7\). Only the first is a possible group size.

Answer: \(8\).

retry.feedback: The smaller factor is the number of options after the first person is chosen.

blocks.html: Name what is being counted in each factor. Multiply successive choices and add only disjoint alternatives.

addmaths-0606-count-arrangements.description: Count arrangements of distinct objects with position and adjacency restrictions.

sections.title: How do fixed places affect an arrangement?
sections.label: End places

blocks.html: Fill restricted positions first. The remaining places use the objects that remain.

blocks.title: Practise the method
blocks.html: If two named objects occupy both ends in either order, count both left–right choices and arrange the middle.

blocks.title: Use the product rule to arrange distinct objects
blocks.prompt: Distinct flags are displayed along a straight rail. There are 7 objects. How many orders are possible with no restriction?
blocks.hint: After each position is filled there is one fewer choice.
blocks.solution:
There are 7 choices for the first place, 6 for the next, and so on down to one.

Multiply these choices to obtain \(7!\).

Answer: \(5040\).

retry.feedback: There are different numbers of choices at each stage. The supply shrinks after each choice.

blocks.html: Filling both end positions uses two objects. They cannot reappear in the middle.

blocks.title: Use the two outside positions
blocks.prompt: Distinct flags are displayed along a straight rail. There are 11 objects. The coral and plum flags occupy the two ends, in either order. How many orders are possible?
blocks.hint: Choose which named object is on each end, then arrange the middle.
blocks.solution:
Choose one of the two named objects for the first end. The second end is then fixed.

Arrange the other 9 objects in the intervening positions.

Answer: \(725760\).

retry.feedback: The named objects can swap ends.

blocks.html: Name what is being counted in each factor. Multiply successive choices and add only disjoint alternatives.

sections.title: How does making a block help?
sections.label: Blocks

blocks.html: A required adjacent group acts as one item when counting its position.

blocks.title: Practise the method
blocks.html: Count the internal arrangements separately and multiply. Put the distinct members back into their block after moving it.

blocks.title: Keep two positions adjacent
blocks.prompt: Distinct flags are displayed along a straight rail. There are 12 objects. The coral and plum flags must be adjacent. How many orders are possible?
blocks.hint: Treat the two named objects as one block, then restore their internal order.
blocks.solution:
Treat the two named objects as a block. Arrange this block and the 10 remaining objects.

Multiply \(11!\) by two because the order inside the block can be reversed.

Answer: \(79833600\).

retry.feedback: This counts each block only once. Both internal orders are allowed.

blocks.html: Treating the pair as a block removes an outside position, not an internal order.

blocks.title: Use the two outside positions
blocks.prompt: Distinct instruments are arranged in a straight display. There are 8 objects. The lute and flute occupy the two ends, in either order. How many orders are possible?
blocks.hint: Choose which named object is on each end, then arrange the middle.
blocks.solution:
Choose one of the two named objects for the first end. The second end is then fixed.

Arrange the other 6 objects in the intervening positions.

Answer: \(1440\).

retry.feedback: The named objects can swap ends.

blocks.html: Name what is being counted in each factor. Multiply successive choices and add only disjoint alternatives.

sections.title: How do I count when two objects must be apart?
sections.label: Separated

blocks.html: Count all arrangements, then subtract those where the pair is adjacent.

blocks.title: Practise the method
blocks.html: The complement is useful because a single block count covers every forbidden adjacent position.

blocks.title: Count only separated pairs
blocks.prompt: Distinct instruments are arranged in a straight display. There are 9 objects. The lute and flute must not be next to one another. How many orders are possible?
blocks.hint: Work out the number of adjacent arrangements and subtract it.
blocks.solution:
All orders give \(9!\). The adjacent pair can be treated as one item, with two possible internal orders.

Subtract \(2\times 8!\) from the unrestricted count.

Answer: \(282240\).

retry.feedback: That counts the excluded arrangements with the pair adjacent.

blocks.html: The words 'not together' describe the complement of the block count.

blocks.title: Keep two positions adjacent
blocks.prompt: Distinct plant pots are placed in a line. There are 5 objects. The mint and thyme pots must be adjacent. How many orders are possible?
blocks.hint: Treat the two named objects as one block, then restore their internal order.
blocks.solution:
Treat the two named objects as a block. Arrange this block and the 3 remaining objects.

Multiply \(4!\) by two because the order inside the block can be reversed.

Answer: \(48\).

retry.feedback: This counts each block only once. Both internal orders are allowed.

addmaths-0606-count-ordered-selections.description: Choose and order a smaller set of distinct objects.

sections.title: When does order change the outcome?
sections.label: Different slots

blocks.html: Use \({}^nP_r=\frac{n!}{(n-r)!}\) for r different roles from n distinct items.

blocks.title: Practise the method
blocks.html: List the roles in a fixed sequence. The second selection has one fewer choice than the first.

blocks.title: Count ordered selections
blocks.prompt: A design studio has 14 distinct mock-ups. In how many ways can the organiser fill 2 labelled places in a display? A candidate or item may be used only once.
blocks.hint: Swapping two occupied places produces a different result.
blocks.solution:
The slots are different, so use \({}^{14}P_{2}\).

Compute \(\frac{14!}{12!}\).

Answer: \(182\).

retry.feedback: That counts sets of choices. Changing the order here changes the result.

blocks.html: A selection rule counts a set only once. It cannot distinguish first place from second place.

blocks.title: Fill a fixed named slot
blocks.prompt: A design studio has 8 distinct mock-ups. To fill 3 labelled places in a display, one particular candidate or item must fill the first slot. How many results are possible?
blocks.hint: Reserve the first slot before counting the remaining slots.
blocks.solution:
Fill the first slot in exactly one way. Choose and order the remaining 2 slots from 7 options.

Use \({}^{7}P_{2}\).

Answer: \(42\).

retry.feedback: That allows any choice in the slot that must be fixed.

blocks.html: Name what is being counted in each factor. Multiply successive choices and add only disjoint alternatives.

sections.title: How does a one-position ban work?
sections.label: Specified slot

blocks.html: A candidate barred from the first slot may still be used later.

blocks.title: Practise the method
blocks.html: Find the total and subtract the orders with that candidate first. Check each permitted later slot still has the right options.

blocks.title: Exclude one assignment to a slot
blocks.prompt: A design studio has 9 distinct mock-ups. To fill 3 labelled places in a display, one particular candidate or item cannot fill the first slot but may fill another slot. How many results are possible?
blocks.hint: Separate the forbidden first-slot assignment from the allowed later assignments.
blocks.solution:
Count all results with \({}^{9}P_{3}\). There are \({}^{8}P_{2}\) results with the restricted item first.

Subtract the restricted results only. The restricted item is allowed in the other slots.

Answer: \(448\).

retry.feedback: That removes the item from all positions.

blocks.html: Removing a candidate from the pool entirely is a stronger restriction.

blocks.title: Count ordered selections
blocks.prompt: A design studio has 13 distinct mock-ups. In how many ways can the organiser fill 3 labelled places in a display? A candidate or item may be used only once.
blocks.hint: Swapping two occupied places produces a different result.
blocks.solution:

Compute \(\frac{13!}{10!}\).

Answer: \(1716\).

retry.feedback: That counts sets of choices. Changing the order here changes the result.

blocks.html: Name what is being counted in each factor. Multiply successive choices and add only disjoint alternatives.

sections.title: How do I include a required item?
sections.label: Must use

blocks.html: Place the required item in one available slot, then order the remaining choices.

blocks.title: Practise the method
blocks.html: A count for one possible position must be multiplied by the number of legal positions. All these cases are disjoint.

blocks.title: Include a specified item somewhere in an order
blocks.prompt: A design studio has 14 distinct mock-ups. To fill 3 labelled places in a display, a named item or candidate must be used. How many results are possible?
blocks.hint: Decide where the required item goes before filling the other places.
blocks.solution:
Choose one of the 3 positions for the specified item.

Order the remaining 2 positions in \({}^{13}P_{2}\) ways and multiply.

Answer: \(468\).

retry.feedback: That assumes the required choice is in one particular position.

blocks.html: A required item is not necessarily fixed in the first slot.

blocks.title: Exclude one assignment to a slot
blocks.prompt: A design studio has 8 distinct mock-ups. To fill 4 labelled places in a display, one particular candidate or item cannot fill the first slot but may fill another slot. How many results are possible?
blocks.hint: Separate the forbidden first-slot assignment from the allowed later assignments.
blocks.solution:
Count all results with \({}^{8}P_{4}\). There are \({}^{7}P_{3}\) results with the restricted item first.

Subtract the restricted results only. The restricted item is allowed in the other slots.

Answer: \(1470\).

retry.feedback: That removes the item from all positions.

extraPractice.hint: Separate the forbidden first-slot assignment from the allowed later assignments.
extraPractice.solution:
Count all results with \({}^{14}P_{3}\). There are \({}^{13}P_{2}\) results with the restricted item first.

Subtract the restricted results only. The restricted item is allowed in the other slots.

Answer: \(2028\).

retry.feedback: That removes the item from all positions.

revision.body:
When does order change the outcome?

Use \({}^nP_r=\frac{n!}{(n-r)!}\) for r different roles from n distinct items.

How does a one-position ban work?

A candidate barred from the first slot may still be used later.

How do I include a required item?

Place the required item in one available slot, then order the remaining choices.

blocks.html: Use \(\binom nr=\frac{n!}{r!(n-r)!}\) when the chosen objects form one set.

blocks.title: Practise the method

blocks.title: Count unordered selections
blocks.prompt: To make garden trials, a curator may choose from 8 distinct herbs and 12 distinct shrubs. Selections of 4 items are unordered. How many different selections are possible with no further restriction?
blocks.hint: Switching the order in which two objects are chosen leaves the same set.
blocks.solution:
Choose 4 of the 20 distinct items. Use \(\binom{20}{4}\).

Divide the ordered count by \(4!\) to account for all the descriptions of the same set.

Answer: \(4845\).

retry.feedback: That counts different orders for the same collection.

blocks.html: Using an ordered formula counts the same selection several times.

blocks.title: Meet an exact two-group quota
blocks.prompt: To make garden trials, a curator may choose from 4 distinct herbs and 5 distinct shrubs. Selections of 5 items are unordered. How many selections contain exactly 2 of the herbs?
blocks.hint: Split the selection into independent choices from the two groups.
blocks.solution:
Choose 2 of the herbs, then 3 of the shrubs.

Both choices are needed, so multiply \(\binom{4}{2}\) by \(\binom{5}{3}\).

Answer: \(60\).

retry.feedback: Adding would describe either one choice or the other. The selection needs both.

blocks.title: Add disjoint selection cases
blocks.prompt: To make display boxes, a curator may choose from 9 distinct wood carvings and 5 distinct stone carvings. Selections of 5 items are unordered. How many selections contain either 1 or 2 of the wood carvings?
blocks.hint: For each exact number, multiply group choices. Then add the disjoint cases.
blocks.solution:
Count the two disjoint cases as \(\binom{9}{1}\binom{5}{4}\) and \(\binom{9}{2}\binom{5}{3}\).

Add the counts \(45\) and \(360\).

Answer: \(405\).

retry.feedback: This gives one of the two allowed cases.

blocks.title: Require at least one from a group
blocks.prompt: To make display boxes, a curator may choose from 10 distinct wood carvings and 5 distinct stone carvings. Selections of 5 items are unordered. How many selections contain at least one of the wood carvings?
blocks.hint: Count selections with no member of the required group.
blocks.solution:
All selections: \(\binom{15}{5}\). Those with none of the wood carvings: \(\binom{5}{5}\).

Discard just that single excluded class.

Answer: \(3002\).

retry.feedback: At least one also includes selections with two or more from the required group.

sections.title: How do I model a reported number of orders?
sections.label: Order equation

blocks.html: Two different labelled positions give n times one fewer than n.

blocks.title: Practise the method
blocks.html: Use the two factors to build a quadratic. The number of people or objects is a positive whole number.

blocks.title: Recover the group size from ordered pairs
blocks.prompt: There are 132 ways to name a first and second person from a group of \(n\) distinct people. Determine \(n\).
blocks.hint: There are n choices first and one fewer second.
blocks.solution:
Use \(n(n-1)=132\).

The roots are \(12\) and \(-11\). Only the first is a possible group size.

Answer: \(12\).

retry.feedback: The smaller factor is the number of options after the first person is chosen.

blocks.html: The value of the smaller factor is the supply after the first choice.

blocks.title: Find the integer in a factorial equation
blocks.prompt: Find the non-negative integer \(r\) for which \(\frac{(r+2)!}{r!}=380\).
blocks.hint: The factorial ratio leaves two consecutive factors.
blocks.solution:
Expand and cancel to obtain \((r+2)(r+1)=380\).

The two consecutive factors are \(19\) and \(20\). The other algebraic root is negative.

Answer: \(18\).

retry.feedback: The smaller factor is one more than the requested value.

sections.title: Why does an unordered pair give half the count?
sections.label: Pair equation

blocks.html: Every unordered pair has two descriptions if you write its members in order.

blocks.title: Practise the method
blocks.html: Divide by two, form the equation, multiply through, then solve for the positive integer.

blocks.title: Recover the group size from pair counts
blocks.prompt: A mixer organiser chooses two different people from a group of \(n\). There are 136 different unordered pairs. Determine \(n\).
blocks.hint: Pairs are unordered. Divide the two-place ordered count by two.
blocks.solution:
Set \(\frac{n(n-1)}{2}=136\).

The roots of the resulting quadratic are \(17\) and \(-16\). The group size must be positive.

Answer: \(17\).

retry.feedback: The product gives consecutive integers. The greater one is the number available.

blocks.html: An ordered pair count is double the number of two-element sets.

blocks.title: Compare successive combination counts
blocks.prompt: Find the value of \(\frac{\binom{33}{6}}{\binom{33}{5}}\) in simplest form.
blocks.hint: Cancel common factorials before multiplying large numbers.
blocks.solution:
Write both combinations using factorials. The common \(33!\) cancels.

The ratio reduces to \(\frac{28}{6}\).

Answer: \(\frac{14}{3}\).

Write both combinations using factorials. The common \(34!\) cancels.

The ratio reduces to \(\frac{29}{6}\).

Answer: \(\frac{29}{6}\).

blocks.html: Preserve the order of the ratio. Reversing numerator and denominator reverses the result.

blocks.title: Cancel a factorial quotient
blocks.prompt: Evaluate \(\frac{15!}{11!}\).
blocks.hint: Expand the numerator only as far as the factorial in the denominator.
blocks.solution:
The common factor is \(11!\). Cancel it.

Multiply the remaining factors: \(15\times14\times13\times12\).

Answer: \(32760\).

retry.feedback: The factor immediately below the last required factor belongs to the cancelled denominator.
